verdicts.critic:
Neutrality is, on the whole, strong and above corpus par. Eight camps against a published-corpus norm of five to six; each steelman is a banner line its own proponents would sign; every position carries a named representative, real proponents, and a prevalence basis grounded in something checkable. The actions ledger gives each of the eight camps exactly one doorway, and all eight URLs resolve live and match their descriptions (Patriotic Millionaires being one clause loose). No house verdict anywhere: where the draft adjudicates, it attributes — "Their counterfactuals put most of the fall on...", "which by this camp's reading they are", "a divergence institutionalists cite as evidence". I verified the load-bearing anchor of every camp against primary sources: Auten-Splinter 8.6%/1962 to 8.8%/2019, Autor-Goldin-Katz 62%/38%, Farber-Herbst-Kuziemko-Naidu's "ten and twenty log points" (quoted almost verbatim from the QJE abstract), De Loecker 21%-to-61% and the Traina SG&A rebuttal, Azar-Marinescu-Steinbaum 17%, Wang-Wilcox 97% and Lerman-Wilcox $6,500/$4,700, Zucman's G20 2%/3,000 payers/$200-250bn/0.3%, Piketty-Saez-Stantcheva's 83%, EPI 27.0%-to-11.6% and the 7.7-point 90/50 decomposition, ProPublica 3.4% and Bezos 1.1% on $127bn (the 2006-2018 window, correctly paired), Chetty's 62%/29% and 80%/71% counterfactuals, Fed DFA 31.6% in 2026Q1 just under the 31.8% record set in 2025Q4, and the Abundance camp's BLS decile shares (top-decile shelter $33,257 against $179,513 of outlays is 18.5%, exactly as claimed, and the 7.7-point spread is "nearly eight points"). That is unusually clean.

The CRUX is the best I have seen in this corpus and I want to say so plainly, since the crux critic it replaces never blocked. It breaks the template the 2026-08-14 corpus check flagged: no trailing question mark, no "or" fork, a declarative that names an axis ("The split runs twice: what pulled the ends apart, then whether the distance is the harm"). It does not compress a multi-camp field into a binary — it names six forces and then a second axis, and every one of the eight camps locates itself: bargaining rules, the skill race, compounding capital, market power, trade, the household, and then Growth First and Abundance under "Two say the measured distance was never the injury." It is honest non-balance, six against two, not theatre. The values field even gives Family Structure its own fair question ("whether a household's own arrangements are a private matter or a public one") rather than folding it into someone else's fight. No house verdict, no "both sides have a point."

Two defects block, and both are the same species: a claim carrying more authority than its sourcing supports, each one propping up a different camp.

First, the topic's headline Basics figure. Basics is defined as facts every camp accepts, and this draft puts the WID pre-tax top 1% series there — then, four positions later, builds a tier-1 camp weighted 60 out of the proposition that exactly this series is wrong. Auten and Splinter find the top 1%'s share of pre-tax national income up about 2.8 points since 1960 against 9.4 points on the fiscal-income measure; Piketty, Saez and Zucman have been answering them in technical notes since 2023. The stat's detail does gesture at a dispute, but it names the 1986 reclassification question, which is a secondary technical quarrel, and stays silent on the primary live one. The effect on a reader is asymmetric framing rather than a bare inaccuracy: Basics reads as the shared floor, so Growth First arrives already contradicted by "the facts" instead of arriving as one side of a dispute the field has not settled. Every other camp's contested anchor is either flagged in place (the productivity-pay gap detail names the AEI deflator critique; the top-tax-rate detail names Tax Foundation against Saez-Zucman) or confined to its own position. This one is not.

Second, the France Stratégie sentence in Capital Tax Egalitarian. This is the camp's answer to the single strongest objection against it, and its force comes entirely from the attribution: not advocates saying the outflows were small, but the French government's own evaluation committee. I could not confirm either half. The €3bn figure that circulates in the French literature is a €3.04bn annual average of assets leaving with departing ISF payers over 2002-2015, which traces to tax-administration and Senate sources rather than to the France Stratégie committee, whose published reports I could reach discuss revenue loss and departure counts (622 payers with €2.3bn in 2016) without the ratio. The 0.4% denominator I could not source at all. Under the project invariant this cannot stand as asserted, and it cannot be handed to the human as homework either.

Everything else I found is polish, and none of it misleads. Worth noting for the record what I checked and cleared: the Basics selection does lean, with nine of thirteen stats reading as evidence for the widening side, but the CBO after-tax series is tier 1 and carries its own 2019-versus-2021 caveat, and the charged items (CEO ratio, statutory top rate) each carry a counter in their detail, so the section informs rather than argues. The Worker Power detail is the only tier-1 position with no external counter, but its counters do appear in Q1 and Q5, so a reader meets them. And on missing camps: I searched the 2026 landscape and it maps cleanly onto these eight — the oligarchy/populist, abundance and affordability camps now organizing the argument all have homes here. The two candidates I could name (meritocratic sorting and opportunity hoarding, per Markovits, Sandel and Reeves; and the immigration-supply diagnosis, per Borjas and CIS) are second-tier, and neither omission tilts the page in a direction, so neither blocks.

notes: Crux, for the record: this is the strongest crux in the corpus and should be left alone. It is the first published-quality lead that does not end in '?' and does not use an 'or' fork, which is exactly the template failure the 2026-08-14 corpus check flagged across 11 of 11 topics. Six-forces-then-two is honest non-balance, and all eight camps locate themselves in the subtitle axis.

Basics selection leans, without misleading. Nine of thirteen stats read as evidence for the widening/institutionalist side; Growth First gets one (CBO), Skills one, Trade one, Abundance one, and Market Power and Family Structure get none, while five other camps have a shared-fact anchor. The charged items each carry a counter in their detail, so this informs rather than argues — but if a stat is ever swapped in, the single-parent-household share (a genuinely shared descriptive fact) would give Family Structure the anchor it currently lacks.

Worker Power Institutionalist is the only tier-1 position whose detail carries no external counter — Growth First gets a full critics paragraph, Capital Tax gets the French repeal, Market Power gets Traina, Family Structure gets endogeneity, Skills gets the SF Fed stall, Trade gets the automation skeptics. The counters to this camp do appear in Q1 and Q5, so no reader is misled; noting only because the pattern is otherwise so consistent. The natural one-clause addition would be that the minimum-wage employment literature remains contested (Neumark and Wascher's payroll-record reanalysis) alongside Card and Krueger.

Lean-label to paragraph ordering is inverted in two questions. Q1, Q2, Q4, Q5, Q7 and Q8 all put the lean_label_a side in the first detail paragraph; Q3 labels A 'Overstated' but opens with 'The still-real side', and Q9 labels A 'Distribution' but opens with 'The living-costs case'. Since the lean bar is a reveal mechanism, a reader mapping the bar to the prose will map it backwards on those two.

Q6 names three targets in its text and works all three in its detail (top, floor, middle) but offers a two-pole lean axis ('Cap the top' / 'Floor first'), leaving the middle target — the one the Worker Power and Trade Shock camps are pointed at — with no pole to sit on.

Q2's why opens 'This is the fork the whole topic turns on', ranking one question above the other eight. It is an editorial ranking rather than a verdict on the answer, and the sentence that follows actually states the conditional side more fully than the inherent side, so it tilts mildly rightward rather than leftward — but the crux already carries this axis, so the superlative is not needed.

Market Power Trustbuster is the only position missing `prevalence_basis` (and `color_key`), so its weight of 55 is the one prevalence figure with no stated justification while the other seven are all grounded. Structural rather than neutral, but it is the sort of gap that reads as the camp being handled more lightly.

scope_covered promises 'income and wealth gaps in rich democracies' and the overview says 'rich-world', but twelve of thirteen Basics stats and seven of eight positions are US-framed. The cross-country redistribution stat is the only real non-US anchor. Either narrow the scope wording to the United States, or the non-US material has to grow to match the promise.

The Patriotic Millionaires action describes the group as lobbying 'for a coordinated global minimum tax on billionaires', but the linked priorities page covers domestic capital and inheritance taxation only. Either link the org's international/global-tax page or drop that clause, so the description matches the page it points at.

On camp coverage, for a future editor rather than this draft: the two candidates I found and judged non-blocking are the meritocratic-sorting and opportunity-hoarding diagnosis (Markovits, Sandel, Reeves — elite credential sorting and assortative mating as the engine, which is a genuinely different diagnosis from Skills Race's 'more education narrows the gap') and the immigration-supply diagnosis (Borjas, CIS). Neither is first-tier in the 2026 landscape, the corpus norm is five to six positions against this draft's eight, and neither omission tilts the page in a direction. If a ninth is ever added, meritocratic sorting is the stronger candidate.

verdicts.critic: Eight positions, and seven of them are genuinely endorsable: each opens in its own voice with a claim its proponents actually make, carries hard numbers I could verify against primary sources, and handles its own internal splits without conceding the frame. Spot-verification was unusually clean. I confirmed against primaries: Autor/Goldin/Katz's 62%/38% supply-vs-demand decomposition (NBER w26705, verbatim, including the 1939-79 benchmark); Goldin & Katz's supply counterfactual (BPEA 2007: "the deceleration in relative supply growth more than fully explains the post-1980 rise"); Auten & Splinter's 8.6%→8.8% after-tax top-1% share and their own words "a modest 0.2 percentage point" (JPE); Piketty-Saez-Stantcheva's 83% optimal rate (NBER w17616); Farber/Herbst/Kuziemko/Naidu's ten-to-twenty log-point premium and the mid-1930s-to-late-1940s compression (NBER w24587, verbatim); EPI's 27.0%→11.6% coverage and the 7.7-point 90/50 widening; ProPublica's $401bn/3.4% and Bezos's $127bn/1.1% (2006-2018, fetched from the article); France Stratégie's €3bn / 0.4%; Zucman's G20 2%, $200-250bn, ~3,000 people, 0.3%; De Loecker-Eeckhout-Unger 21%→61%; Philippon's $5,000; Azar-Marinescu-Steinbaum's 17% on posted wages; Traina's SG&A correction; ADH's bottom-four-deciles wage result and the 2021 persistence-to-2019 finding; Wang-Wilcox 97%; Lerman-Wilcox $6,500/$4,700; Chetty et al. 2014 verbatim ("the single strongest correlate ... among all the variables we explored"); the SF Fed 2025 paper's demand-side attribution; the Hayek Book Prize; and the Open Markets June 2026 convening. The Abundance Builder's BLS shelter-share stat I recomputed from the BLS public API: 8,287/31,660 = 26.2% and 33,257/179,513 = 18.5%, a 7.7-point gap — "nearly eight points" is exact. All eight action URLs return 200. No house verdict: the crux names the double split without resolving it, and the basics set, while tilted toward "the gap is large," carries the CBO after-tax series at tier 1 and hangs a dissent inside almost every detail (the 1986 reclassification debate, AEI on deflators, Tax Foundation against Saez-Zucman). Three defects fail it. The first is the one that matters most for this dimension: the Trade Shock Reindustrialist lists Autor, Dorn and Hanson as proponents of a camp defined by tariffs and industrial policy. Autor says the administration is "arriving at the wrong answers" on manufacturing, and his own 2024 work finds no positive employment effect from the 2018-19 import tariffs. That misdescribes three real people's positions, and it also weakens the camp by crediting its prescription to researchers who reject it instead of to the advocates who hold it. The second inverts the Family Structure camp's best rebuttal: as written, Kearney "answers" the endogeneity charge with evidence that economic shocks preceded marriage decline, which is the critics' arrow, not hers. Her actual natural experiment (Kearney & Wilson on the fracking boom) found local booms in less-educated men's earnings raised births but not marriage — evidence that cuts the other way. The camp's strongest card is being played face-down. The third is an unverified contested fact in the Abundance Builder's banner paragraph: Houston and Tokyo "show housing costs can hold flat even as demand climbs." Tokyo's flat real rents are contested in the literature as a post-bubble artifact, and Houston prices have risen substantially; the position's own detail states the supportable version ("kept homebuilding roughly in step with population and job growth"), so the description is reaching past its own evidence. For parity: the published Supply Liberalizer position on housing-affordability-crisis carries Auckland's 23% and Pew's 1.4 points, which is the standard this sentence should meet. On missing camps, I searched for what is absent: monetary policy and asset-price inflation, financialization, assortative mating, immigration, superstar effects. Assortative mating and superstar effects are mechanisms without an advocacy program; immigration's measured contribution is small in the literature; the monetary/asset-price camp is the only genuine candidate for a ninth, and its absence does not mislead a reader given eight steelmanned camps spanning -3 to +3. That is a note, not a block.

blocking.issue: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are listed as proponents of the Trade Shock Reindustrialist position, whose defining prescription is tariffs, procurement rules and industrial policy. They are the camp's evidentiary source, not its advocates, and Autor publicly rejects the prescription: he argues the tariff push is "arriving at the wrong answers" on manufacturing, and his own 2024 study of the 2018-19 tariffs finds no positive employment effect from US import tariffs (negative effects from retaliation). This misstates the stated positions of three named real people, and it simultaneously weakens the camp by attributing its program to researchers who disown it rather than to the advocates who actually hold it. It also sits oddly beside Autor's correct listing as representative of the Skills Race Theorist.
blocking.fix: Remove "David Autor, David Dorn, Gordon Hanson, " from the Trade Shock Reindustrialist proponents string, leaving "Robert Scott (Economic Policy Institute), Oren Cass, Michael Stumo (Coalition for a Prosperous America)" and adding the advocacy organizations the detail already names (United Steelworkers, American Compass). The detail paragraph already frames ADH correctly as the research that "broke that consensus," so nothing substantive is lost; representative_name "Oren Cass" is already right.

blocking.issue: The Family Structure Analyst's rebuttal to the endogeneity charge is stated backwards, so the camp's strongest answer reads as a concession to its critics. Evidence that "economic shocks preceded marriage decline" is the reverse-causation story the critics are pressing, not a reply to it. Kearney's actual natural-experiment evidence (Kearney & Wilson on the fracking boom) runs the other way: local booms that raised the earnings of non-college men increased births but did not raise marriage rates or reduce single motherhood, contrary to the "marriageable men" prediction. As drafted, a real proponent would not endorse this sentence, because it hands the critics the causal arrow while purporting to answer them.
blocking.fix: Replace the clause with what Kearney actually found, e.g.: "Kearney answers with the fracking boom, where a local surge in the earnings of men without a degree raised births but left marriage rates and single motherhood unmoved, which she reads as evidence the retreat from marriage is not simply downstream of men's wages" — then keep the existing concession ("the camp concedes the causal arrows likely run both ways, and treats family stability as a lever worth pulling regardless") as written.
blocking.quote: "Kearney answers by pointing to natural experiments where economic shocks preceded marriage decline in a region or cohort" — Family Structure Analyst, detail

blocking.issue: The Abundance Builder's description asserts, as demonstrated, that Houston and Tokyo show housing costs "can hold flat even as demand climbs." This is a contested fact about the world, not a claim about what the camp believes, so the camp's own material does not license it. I could not verify it: Tokyo's flat real rents are attributed by critics to the post-1992 bubble collapse and subsequent stagnation rather than to zoning, and Houston single-family prices have risen substantially over the period (recent reporting frames a $322k median as a multi-year low, not a flat series). The position's own detail states the supportable version and the description overshoots it.
blocking.fix: Soften the description to what the detail and the sources support: cut "hold flat" and say that both places kept homebuilding roughly in step with population and job growth, holding prices far below comparably booming, tightly zoned metros — which is the claim the Glaeser-Gyourko zoning-tax wedge in the detail actually carries. If a hard number is wanted at parity with the published corpus, use a sourced upzoning result rather than a qualitative "flat."
blocking.quote: "Places that let supply expand, from Houston’s light-touch zoning to Tokyo’s uniform by-right rules, show housing costs can hold flat even as demand climbs." — Abundance Builder, description

notes: Market Power Trustbuster is the only position missing prevalence_basis and color_key; the other seven carry both. The published corpus (nuclear-energy.gold, housing-affordability-crisis, universal-basic-income) omits prevalence_basis entirely, so this is internal inconsistency within the draft rather than a parity gap — but the weight of 55 should get the same one-line justification its peers have.

Family Structure Analyst's steelman, "Family stability predicts a child’s income better than the tax code does," makes a comparison the underlying evidence never runs: Chetty et al. compare single-parent share against school quality, residential segregation, social capital and local inequality, not against tax policy. "Better than the school or the tax bracket" would be both punchier and supported.

The same position's description says the finding predicts "a poor child’s chances of reaching the top of the income distribution." The Chetty measure is absolute upward mobility — mean income rank at 25 for children of 25th-percentile parents — not the odds of reaching the top.

Growth First Economist's description pins the measurement error on "Census surveys," but its headline evidence (Auten & Splinter) corrects the tax-record series of Piketty-Saez-Zucman, not Census. The detail sorts the two critiques out correctly; the description collapses them into one and could name both.

Growth First anchors on a 2019 endpoint. Auten & Splinter's own 2025 update runs to 2022 and reports that both pre-tax and after-tax top 1% shares rose another percentage point since 2019, while arguing that adjusting for missing top income in the 1960s leaves "no change ... between 1962 and 2022." The 2019 figure is accurately dated, but the camp's newest framing is more current and no weaker.

Worker Power Institutionalist says the minimum wage lost "about 40%" of its real value since 1968. EPI's own number is roughly 42%, and against a $12.62 (2026 dollars) peak the figure is ~43% — the camp is understating its own grievance.

Capital Tax Egalitarian's detail runs four em dashes across two paragraphs, against the house guidance to keep the em dash for punch that earns it. Two of them are doing work a colon or a new sentence would do better.

No camp carries the monetary-policy and asset-price explanation (QE and asset inflation as a driver of wealth concentration — e.g. Karen Petrou's Engine of Inequality, and its hard-money counterpart on the right). It is the most defensible ninth camp; assortative mating and superstar effects are mechanisms without an advocacy program, and immigration's measured contribution to the wage-inequality rise is small in the literature. Eight steelmanned camps spanning -3 to +3 is broad coverage and the omission does not mislead, so this is a suggestion, not a defect.

Each is decodable from context and each is properly unpacked in its detail; listed so the human can decide whether to plain-word the first one.

Crux and question compact copy sit at the right bar throughout; the only term-of-art openings ("Decomposition:" in crux empirical, "compress the distribution" in the T3 question, "erode the base" in the T4 question) are in expanded or below-fold copy where the register allows them.

prevalence_basis.name: Worker Power Institutionalist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Anchors a large empirical literature on unions, minimum wages and the pay-productivity gap, backed by labor-aligned research institutes; minimum-wage and bargaining law is a standing legislative item across rich democracies.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Falling union density, an eroded wage floor and top-rate tax cuts shifted bargaining power upward; rebuild the institutions and the gap narrows.

prevalence_basis.name: Skills Race Theorist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: The default explanation in labor economics for four decades, heavily cited and matched by an education-and-training footprint in national policy; now extended to evidence on AI exposure by occupation.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Technology kept raising the return to skill faster than schooling supplied it, so the repair is education, training and adapting to what AI shifts next.

prevalence_basis.name: Capital Tax Egalitarian
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: One of the most-cited economics books of the century, plus an active G20 track on a minimum effective tax for billionaires publicly backed by several heads of government and finance ministries.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Returns on capital outrun growth, so wealth concentrates by arithmetic unless taxed; the target is inherited and lightly taxed capital, not wages.

prevalence_basis.name: Growth First Economist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Institutional backing from market-liberal think tanks and a contested top-share series produced by Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation economists that top journals have been arguing over since 2024.
prevalence_basis.sketch: After taxes, transfers and untaxed income are counted the top’s rise is far smaller than headlines suggest; absolute living standards and mobility are the measures that matter.

prevalence_basis.name: Trade Shock Reindustrialist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: The “China shock” papers are among the most-cited empirical work in the field, and tariffs plus industrial policy have been live statute rather than proposal in the US since 2025.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Import competition and offshoring destroyed the middle rungs of the wage ladder; rebuilding domestic production is what puts them back.

prevalence_basis.name: Abundance Builder
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Thin in the older inequality literature but rising fast: a 2025 bestseller translated into cost-of-living policy blueprints and affordability platforms through the 2026 cycle.
prevalence_basis.sketch: What squeezes households is the price of housing, care and energy; build supply and the gap stops biting even where it does not close.

prevalence_basis.name: Family Structure Analyst
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: A smaller footprint in economics than in sociology and family policy, sustained by a prominent 2023 book on two-parent households and durable conservative policy backing.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Household inequality tracks who partners with, and stays with, whom; family formation and stability drive how far children climb.
